Yes, the story has an appropriate balance between scene and summary/exposition. 

The narrative unfolds primarily as a single, vivid scene in real-time on the ferry dock, driven by sparse dialogue and physical actions (e.g., cars rolling off the ramp, wiping the railing, untying the rope). Woven seamlessly into the pauses of this scene are brief moments of exposition and summary. Instead of halting the story with long blocks of backstory, the writer uses Ilse's internal observations to naturally deliver crucial background information—such as her decades of working the river, Jonas's resemblance to Henning, the routine of the ferry (the red van that always waits, the eleven-minute crossing), and the unspoken history of estrangement between the two characters. This careful integration keeps the pacing tight and the emotional tension high while still giving the reader all the context needed to understand the weight of their reunion.
